p: 'I would not make the charge now,' he had written in a later message. 'But the order has been given and the troops are already moving.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 13 of 14

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 14 of 14

p: Lewis Armistead and Winfield Hancock had been friends since before the war — close friends, the kind of friends that the old army made of men who served together in remote posts for years. When Virginia seceded, Armistead had gone south. On the night before he left California, at a farewell party, he had placed his hands on Hancock's shoulders and wept. 'Hancock, goodbye,' he said. 'You can never know what this has cost me.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 1 of 11

p: That was two years before Gettysburg.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 2 of 11

p: Now Armistead led what remained of his Virginia brigade across the open ground toward Cemetery Ridge. The cannonade had cleared some of the Union guns. There was a gap — a real gap — in the line ahead, near a low stone wall and a copse of trees.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 3 of 11

p: Armistead placed his black felt hat on the tip of his sword, raising it above his head as a guide for his men in the smoke and confusion. He walked forward — not ran, walked, with a deliberate stride. Ahead was the wall.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 4 of 11

p: He stepped over the wall. Behind him, perhaps 150 men followed.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 5 of 11

p: Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing had been serving his last two guns at that wall all afternoon, wounded twice already, holding the battery together through sheer will. When Armistead's men came over the wall, Cushing was at his gun. He was shot through the mouth and killed.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 6 of 11

p: Armistead reached out and touched one of Cushing's guns. A moment later he was shot — the exact details are disputed, but he fell within the Union lines, beyond the wall.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 7 of 11

p: He was carried to the Union rear. As he lay dying, he asked for Hancock to be brought to him. He did not know that Hancock, on the other side of the ridge, had been wounded almost simultaneously — a nail and saddle pommel fragment driven deep into his thigh.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 8 of 11

p: Both men lay bleeding. The Confederacy had reached its High Water Mark.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 9 of 11

p: Armistead died two days later. He never saw Hancock again.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 10 of 11

p: The stone wall at The Angle, the copse of trees behind it, and the ground where Armistead fell are preserved today exactly as they were on the afternoon of July 3, 1863. A monument marks the spot where he went down.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Armistead at The Angle”, paragraph 11 of 11

p: At one o'clock in the afternoon, two signal guns fired from Seminary Ridge.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The sound was heard in Pittsburgh. Some accounts place it as far as Philadelphia — 140 miles to the east. The smoke rising from Seminary Ridge was visible for twenty miles. Every gun in Alexander's command, every gun in the Third Corps artillery, every piece that could bear on Cemetery Ridge fired simultaneously and continued firing.
